title: Stationary waves

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Explain and use the principle of superposition; understand the experiments that demonstrate stationary waves with microwaves, stretched strings and air columns; explain the formation of a stationary wave graphically, identifying nodes and antinodes; and find a wavelength from the positions of nodes or antinodes.

blocks.heading: The principle of superposition
blocks.text: When two or more waves meet at a point, the resultant displacement at that point is the sum of the displacements that each wave alone would produce there at that instant. Displacement here means the distance of a point of the medium from its rest position — the wave sense of the word, used throughout this topic — with a sign to show which side of the rest position the point sits. The displacements may be of any size and either sign: two displacements of the same sign add to a larger one, and an upward and an equal downward displacement sum to zero.

blocks.heading: What the meeting does, and does not do
blocks.text: Superposition is momentary. Where the two displacements have the same sign the resultant is larger than either alone (constructive); where they have opposite signs it is smaller (destructive), and equal opposite displacements cancel exactly. The instant passes and each wave carries on: after two waves have met and superposed, each continues onwards with its original amplitude, speed and frequency unchanged, as though the other were not there. The resultant intensity at a point follows from the resultant displacement, and intensity is proportional to the square of the amplitude — so overlapping waves do not add their intensities.

blocks.heading: Worked example: two pulses on a skipping rope
blocks.text: Leena and Sipho flick opposite ends of a stretched skipping rope. At the moment the two pulses pass the same point, Leena's pulse alone would hold the rope 4.0 cm above its rest line and Sipho's alone would hold it 1.5 cm below. The resultant displacement is the sum: 4.0 cm upwards together with 1.5 cm downwards leaves 2.5 cm upwards, because 4.0 − 1.5 = 2.5. A moment later the pulses have passed through each other and travel on unchanged, Leena's still 4.0 cm tall and Sipho's still 1.5 cm deep.

blocks.heading: Add displacements, not amplitudes or intensities
blocks.text: A common error is to add the amplitudes, or the intensities, of two overlapping waves. Superposition adds displacements at each point at each instant. The amplitude of the resultant at a point is the largest displacement the sum reaches there, and the intensity follows from that amplitude squared. The test: is it displacements that are added? If a learner has added two amplitudes or two intensities, the principle has been applied to the wrong quantities.

blocks.heading: Microwaves reflected from a metal plate
blocks.text: A microwave transmitter is aimed straight at a flat metal plate. The plate reflects the wave, so two waves of the same frequency travel in opposite directions along the same line and superpose: a stationary wave is set up between transmitter and plate. A probe receiver connected to a meter is moved slowly along the line, and the reading rises and falls — a maximum at an antinode, a minimum (zero or close to it) at a node. The distance across several node-to-node gaps is measured with a ruler; each gap is half a wavelength, so the wavelength follows by doubling the per-gap spacing. With the wave speed known — microwaves travel at 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ — the frequency then follows from the wave equation v = fλ met in topic 7.

blocks.heading: Stretched strings and air columns
blocks.text: A long string is fixed at both ends and driven by a vibration generator. At particular frequencies the string shows points that stay still while the segments between them swing: a stationary wave, formed because the wave from the generator and its reflection from the fixed end travel in opposite directions. For an air column, a tuning fork is held at the mouth of a tube whose length is changed by sliding it in a deeper or shallower pan of water. At some lengths the note grows loud: the column then carries a stationary wave with a node at the water surface and an antinode at the open mouth, and the fork's driving matches a frequency at which the column naturally sounds — resonance.

blocks.heading: Stationary waves, nodes and antinodes
blocks.text: A stationary wave is the pattern formed where two waves of the same frequency travelling in opposite directions superpose. A node is a point where the amplitude is zero; an antinode is a point where the amplitude is greatest. The nodes and antinodes stay in fixed places — the pattern does not travel along — and the wave transfers no energy along the medium, unlike the progressive waves of topic 7. A node forms at a fixed plate or a fixed end; the open mouth of an air column sits at an antinode.

blocks.heading: Explaining the formation graphically
blocks.text: To see why the nodes exist, draw the two waves separately at several instants. Take two identical waves of amplitude A travelling in opposite directions, and draw them at times separated by a quarter of a period. At each chosen instant, add the two displacements point by point along the length to draw the resultant. At certain points the two curves are equal and opposite at each instant drawn: the resultant there is zero at every instant — a node. Halfway between neighbouring nodes the two displacements are equal at every instant, adding to 2A when both are largest — an antinode. The resultant, drawn at several instants, keeps the same nodes while its antinodes oscillate: that envelope is the signature of a stationary wave, and a sketch graph of it with the nodes marked is the standard way the pattern is shown.

blocks.heading: Finding the wavelength from the node pattern
blocks.text: Neighbouring nodes are half a wavelength apart; neighbouring antinodes are half a wavelength apart too; a node and the next antinode are a quarter of a wavelength apart. So one node-to-node measurement gives λ = 2 × spacing. A better method measures across many gaps: with 6 node-to-node gaps spanning 14.4 cm, each gap is 14.4 ÷ 6 = 2.40 cm and λ = 2 × 2.40 = 4.80 cm. The longer the span measured, the smaller the percentage uncertainty a single ruler reading contributes, because the reading's uncertainty is spread across a larger distance. The same numbers come from antinode positions.

blocks.heading: A stationary wave is not two-source interference
blocks.text: A stationary wave is sometimes described as if it were the two-source interference pattern of sub-topic 8.3. It is not. The two waves that form a stationary wave travel in opposite directions — most often a wave and its own reflection — and the pattern is fixed in place. Two-source interference is formed by waves from two separate side-by-side sources travelling onward the same way, and its pattern spreads out from between the sources. The test: are the two waves travelling towards each other? If they are, a stationary wave is forming; if they travel onward side by side, it is a two-source pattern.

blocks.heading: A node is a quarter of a wavelength from the next antinode
blocks.text: The distance from a node to the next antinode is a quarter of a wavelength, not half. A learner who doubles a node-to-antinode distance has halved the wavelength. The safe rule is to work from node to node: that spacing is λ/2. The test: node to node, or node to antinode? Node to node is λ/2, safe to double; node to antinode is λ/4, to be multiplied by four; doubling is right for the first and wrong for the second.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: This section leans on topic 7: progressive waves, the wave equation v = fλ, and phase and phase difference. Interference (sub-topics 8.2 and 8.3) is the other face of superposition. The measuring skills used here — spacing readings across many gaps, and their uncertainties — are practised fully in topic 12.
